concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Triggering Grounds of Article 356
key_dimensions: Two distinct grounds: 'government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution' vs. receipt of Governor's Report vs. President's own satisfaction (President can act without Governor's Report)
Distinction between Article 356 (State Emergency) and Article 365 (failure to comply with Union directions) as a triggering mechanism
UPSC trap: President can proclaim even without Governor's report — 'otherwise' clause in Article 356(1)
Comparison with Article 355 — Union's duty to protect states, and how it precedes/enables Article 356

concepts.name: Role of the Governor in Recommending President's Rule
key_dimensions: Governor's report as the primary but not exclusive trigger — constitutional text says 'on receipt of report or otherwise'
Controversy over 'pocket veto' and partisan use of Governor's discretion in recommending President's Rule
Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission recommendations on restricting Governor's discretionary role
UPSC trap: Governor's report is not binding on the President, nor is it a mandatory prerequisite

concepts.name: Parliamentary Approval and Duration of President's Rule
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within 2 months by simple majority — UPSC trap: NOT a special majority unlike Article 368
Initial duration: 6 months; can be extended up to a maximum of 3 years with parliamentary approval every 6 months

Special condition for extension beyond 1 year: two conditions must BOTH be satisfied — National Emergency in operation in the whole country or that state, AND Election Commission certifies elections cannot be held
UPSC trap: After the 44th Amendment, extension beyond 1 year requires BOTH conditions simultaneously, not either/or

concepts.name: Consequences and Executive Powers During President's Rule
key_dimensions: President assumes functions of State Government; Governor carries on administration on behalf of President
Parliament legislates for the state — laws made by Parliament during President's Rule remain operative even after revocation until altered by State Legislature
UPSC trap: State Legislature is suspended/dissolved — Lok Sabha can pass state legislation even when not in session via ordinance route through President
High Court's position is unaffected — Article 356 does not suspend constitutional provisions relating to High Courts

concepts.name: Revocation of President's Rule — Procedure and Constraints
key_dimensions: Revocation by Presidential Proclamation — does NOT require parliamentary approval (unlike imposition which does)
UPSC trap: Revocation can be done by President on his own; no resolution needed in Parliament
Bommai judgment: Court can order revocation if imposition is found unconstitutional; floor test must precede dissolution
Dissolved vs. suspended State Legislature — implications for revocation and reconstitution

concepts.name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) — Landmark Judicial Intervention
key_dimensions: Nine-judge bench: Presidential proclamation under Article 356 is justiciable and subject to judicial review
Doctrine of floor test: Majority must be tested on floor of House before Governor recommends dismissal; Governor cannot make subjective assessment
Court can restore dissolved State Assembly if proclamation is found mala fide or unconstitutional — restorability principle
UPSC trap: Bommai did NOT make Article 356 non-justiciable; it made it MORE justiciable; also secularism declared a basic feature in this case

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Article 356 — Scope, Limits, and Standards
key_dimensions: Pre-Bommai position: Article 356 was largely non-justiciable (State of Rajasthan v. Union of India, 1977)
Post-Bommai: Justiciable on grounds of mala fide, irrelevant/extraneous considerations, or no material at all
Court cannot go into 'sufficiency' of material but can check 'existence' of material — distinction critical for MCQs
Limitation: Court cannot restore legislature if it has been dissolved after approval by Parliament (Bommai caveat)

concepts.name: Conditions Under Which President's Rule Can Be Extended Beyond One Year
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment (1978) introduced the dual-condition lock for extension beyond 1 year — both conditions must coexist
Condition 1: National Emergency (Article 352) must be in operation in the whole of India OR in the whole or part of that state
Condition 2: Election Commission must certify that general elections to the State Legislature cannot be held
UPSC trap: Absence of either condition makes extension beyond 1 year unconstitutional — this is a hard constitutional limit

concepts.name: Suspension vs. Dissolution of State Legislature Under Article 356
key_dimensions: President can either suspend or dissolve the State Legislative Assembly — two distinct options with different consequences
UPSC trap: President cannot dissolve the Assembly before Parliament approves the proclamation — it can only be suspended till then (Bommai principle reinforced by constitutional convention)
Dissolved Assembly cannot be restored by court; suspended Assembly can be — critical distinction
Legislative Council (Upper House) is NOT subject to dissolution under Article 356 — only Assembly can be dissolved

concepts.name: Sarkaria Commission Recommendations on Article 356
key_dimensions: Article 356 should be used as a 'last resort' — all other possibilities of forming a government must be exhausted
Recommended a warning to the erring state government before invoking Article 356
Governor should not be a political person and should act as a neutral constitutional functionary
UPSC trap: Sarkaria recommendations are NOT legally binding but are treated as constitutional conventions and frequently cited by courts including in Bommai

concepts.name: Punchhi Commission Recommendations on Article 356
key_dimensions: Recommended 'localized emergency' — President's Rule should be localized to specific areas where breakdown has occurred, not extended to entire state mechanically
Suggested a statutory 'inter-state council' mechanism to deliberate before invoking Article 356
Recommended fixed tenure for Governors and limiting discretionary powers regarding house dissolution
UPSC trap: Punchhi Commission (2010) gave more recent and specific recommendations vs. Sarkaria (1988) — both are relevant but Punchhi is more contemporary

concepts.name: Comparison: Article 356 vs. Article 352 vs. Article 360 — Three Types of Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 352: National Emergency — external aggression/armed rebellion; affects Centre-State relations broadly; special majority required
Article 356: State Emergency/President's Rule — constitutional breakdown in state; simple majority for approval; affects only that state
Article 360: Financial Emergency — threat to financial stability of India or any part; has never been proclaimed
UPSC trap: Article 356 approval requires simple majority, NOT special majority — common confusion with Article 352 which requires special majority + absolute majority

concepts.name: Article 356 and Federalism — Constitutional and Political Dimensions
key_dimensions: Article 356 as the 'anti-federal' provision — converts India into a unitary state for that state temporarily
Ambedkar's assurance in Constituent Assembly: Article 356 would be a 'dead letter' — contrast with actual use (100+ times)
Misuse pattern: Mostly used against opposition-ruled states — documented in Sarkaria and Punchhi reports
Bommai judgment's federalism protection: Secularism as basic feature means states promoting communalism can attract Article 356, but it must be genuine

concepts.name: Constituent Assembly Debates on Article 356 — Original Intent vs. Practice
key_dimensions: Dr. Ambedkar: Hoped Article 356 would never be used; described it as a 'safety valve' of last resort
Article 356 modeled on Section 93 of Government of India Act, 1935 — colonial origins
Original draft had no judicial review contemplated — courts later read it in
UPSC angle: Gap between Ambedkar's vision (dead letter) and political reality (110+ impositions) — governance/ethics dimension

concepts.name: Role of Union Cabinet in Proclamation of Article 356
key_dimensions: 44th Amendment: President cannot act without the written advice of the Council of Ministers — same as Article 74
UPSC trap: President acts on 'aid and advice' of Cabinet; if Cabinet advises wrongly, it is a constitutional breach but President has no independent veto after 44th Amendment
Cabinet's collective responsibility means the decision to invoke Article 356 is a collective political decision
Judicial review indirectly scrutinizes Cabinet's advice through the 'material on record' standard from Bommai

concepts.name: Lapsing of State Laws and Ordinances During and After President's Rule
key_dimensions: Laws made by Parliament for the state during President's Rule continue to be in force even after revocation until amended/repealed by State Legislature
President can promulgate ordinances for the state when Parliament is not in session — these have same force as Parliamentary laws for the state
UPSC trap: State Legislature cannot nullify parliamentary laws passed during President's Rule immediately upon revival — they must go through normal legislative process
Contracts and financial obligations entered during President's Rule are binding on the revived state government

concepts.name: Situations That Justify vs. Do Not Justify Imposition of Article 356 — Constitutional Interpretation
key_dimensions: Justified: Hung assembly with no possibility of coalition, physical breakdown of constitutional machinery, state abetting secessionism
NOT justified: Mere loss of majority without exploring alternatives, political corruption alone, administrative inefficiency (per Bommai guidelines)
UPSC trap: A party losing majority does NOT automatically warrant Article 356 — floor test must be conducted first
Post-election stalemate: Governor must give adequate time for coalition formation before recommending President's Rule

concepts.name: Inter-State Council and Article 356 — Institutional Safeguards
key_dimensions: Article 263 Inter-State Council (set up in 1990) recommended as a consultative body before invoking Article 356
No constitutional compulsion to consult Inter-State Council before Article 356 — it is a recommendatory safeguard
National Integration Council, NDC also discussed in context of Centre-State consultation mechanisms
UPSC trap: Inter-State Council is NOT the same as Zonal Councils; it has a broader mandate under Article 263 and is not a substitute for parliamentary approval of Article 356

concepts.name: President's Rule in Jammu & Kashmir — Special Historical and Legal Context
key_dimensions: Pre-2019: J&K had its own Constitution — 'Governor's Rule' under Section 92 of J&K Constitution preceded Article 356 application
Post-Article 370 abrogation (2019): J&K reorganized into two UTs — President's Rule now applies via Lieutenant Governor mechanism, not Article 356 strictly
UPSC trap: After reorganization, J&K (UT with Legislature) and Ladakh (UT without Legislature) — Article 356 applies differently to UTs with legislatures
Historical misuse: J&K saw multiple impositions of Governor's/President's Rule — subject of political and constitutional controversy

concepts.name: President's Rule in Union Territories — Applicability and Distinction
key_dimensions: Article 356 applies to STATES — Union Territories are governed by Article 239 (President governs through Administrator/LG)
UPSC trap: UTs with Legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K) have their own rules — for Delhi, GNCT Act 1991 and 2023 amendment govern Centre-State tussle, not Article 356
Puducherry has seen President's Rule — but through different procedural pathway since it is a UT with legislature
Distinction: For states, Article 356 is the mechanism; for UTs, President has inherent plenary power under Article 239
